notes: Chancery appeal on TMR rule 31(3) discretion after late counter-statement in trade mark revocation; revocation date and remittal issues are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Lowden v Lowden Guitar: late counter-statement in non-use revocation appeal
key_facts: Lowden Guitar Company applied to revoke George Lowden's LOWDEN device mark for five-year non-use under section 46.
The proprietor's agents served Form TM8 and a counter-statement six days late and filed no evidence of use.
The Registry treated opposition as withdrawn and revoked registration from 20 October 1999, a date earlier than five years after registration completed.
Pumfrey J granted an extension of time to appeal; the company sought amendment to substitute 20 October 2000 as the revocation date.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Chancery Division against the Registrar's decision to revoke UK trade mark registration No 1588546 for non-use.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the 7 May 2004 revocation order was set aside and the application remitted for determination of the amendment application, with the register rectified in the interim.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 31(3) gives the Registrar a discretion whether to treat late opposition as withdrawn, but not to circumvent the unextendable rule 31(2) deadline by admitting late factual evidence; revocation cannot take effect from a date earlier than five years after completion of registration, and amendment of grounds after debarring cannot restart time without a fresh counter-statement period.
legal_issues: Whether the Registrar had jurisdiction to revoke from 20 October 1999
Scope of discretion under TMR rule 31(3) after late filing of counter-statement
Whether the Hearing Officer denied a hearing contrary to rule 54
Whether the Registrar could permit amendment of the statement of grounds without allowing a new counter-statement period
linked_authorities: Firetrace Trade Mark [2002] RPC 15
Pharmedica GmbH's Trade Mark Application [2000] RPC 536

notes: CA civil judgment on lawfulness of withholding a serial killer's autobiography typescript under prison Standing Order 5 and Article 10.

enrichment.short_title: Nilsen v Full Sutton Prison: prisoner autobiography and Article 10
key_facts: Dennis Nilsen, serving whole-life terms for six murders, sought return of a 400-page autobiography typescript held outside prison.
The Secretary of State refused delivery relying on Standing Order 5 paragraph 34(9)(c) restricting publication material about inmates' crimes.
Maurice Kay J dismissed judicial review; Nilsen appealed on vires, Article 10 compatibility and proportionality.
An earlier book by Brian Masters had already published graphic accounts based on Nilsen's disclosures.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from refusal of judicial review of the prison governor's decision to withhold the manuscript.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Restrictions on prisoners publishing accounts of their own crimes are a legitimate incident of penal imprisonment within section 47 powers and compatible with Article 10 where narrowly drawn with exceptions for serious representations about conviction or the penal system; withholding the typescript was proportionate despite copies existing outside prison.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 34 falls within powers conferred by the Prison Act
Whether the restriction is prescribed by law and necessary in a democratic society under Article 10
Whether application to incoming correspondence was lawful
Whether withholding was disproportionate given prior publication and external copies

notes: Solicitor negligence appeal on incomplete advice about notice to quit in housing possession; causation and Chester distinguished.

enrichment.short_title: White v Paul Davidson: solicitor negligence and notice to quit causation
key_facts: After his father's death the appellant defended possession proceedings brought by New Downlands Housing Association.
Solicitors advised on mandatory Ground 7 but failed to warn that a notice to quit served on the Public Trustee had already terminated the tenancy.
The landlord amended to rely on the notice to quit; the district judge allowed amendment but ordered the landlord to pay the appellant's costs to date.
The appellant pursued the case despite advice, was later summarily evicted, and sued his former solicitors for fees and damages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from county court judgment for solicitors on their fees claim and dismissal of the client's counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the appellant failed on causation and could not deny solicitors their fees for work done pursuant to instructions.
enrichment.ratio: Where the complaint is failure to give complete advice rather than positively incorrect advice, the client must show on the balance of probabilities he would have acted differently if fully advised; Chester v Afshar does not displace that requirement in solicitor negligence, and incomplete advice keeping hopeless litigation alive does not void entitlement to fees.
legal_issues: Whether solicitors were negligent in not advising on the notice to quit effect
Distinction between failing to advise and giving incorrect advice for causation
Whether the client would have acted differently if properly advised
Applicability of Chester v Afshar to legal professional negligence
Whether negligent advice voided solicitors' entitlement to fees
linked_authorities: Bristol & West Building Society v Mothew [1998] Ch 1
Boateng v Hughmans [2002] PN449
Chester v Afshar [2004] UKHL 41

notes: Mid-trial TCC ruling allowing late witness statements after cross-examination raised implicit dishonesty allegations; trial adjourned.

enrichment.short_title: Sainsbury v WSP: late evidence after implied dishonesty at TCC trial
key_facts: Sainsbury claimed WSP's inadequate foundation design caused expenditure on a replacement Newhaven supermarket.
Defendants' cross-examination suggested the claimants decided to rebuild much earlier than their January 2003 case.
Claimants sought to add witness statements from finance and risk directors and a supplemental statement from Nicholas Jones.
Defendants objected that new evidence would remedy deficiencies exposed in cross-examination of earlier witnesses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory ruling during trial in the Technology and Construction Court on permission to adduce additional witness evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants permitted to rely on the new statements and disputed passage; trial adjourned until Monday week to allow recall of witnesses and preparation of further cross-examination.
enrichment.ratio: Where cross-examination fairly raised an implicit allegation that claimants concealed the timing of a critical commercial decision, justice may require allowing late evidence on how that decision was taken, coupled with adjournment and opportunity to recall witnesses and inspect further documents.
legal_issues: Whether late witness statements should be admitted mid-trial
Whether new evidence was an improper attempt to repair cross-examination damage
Effect of privilege claims on transparency of the claimants' case
Whether witnesses should be recalled after new evidence

notes: Long Crim CA judgment refusing to vacate manslaughter guilty plea; Hall/Turner principles and later Croft witness developments.

enrichment.short_title: R v Mason: application to vacate manslaughter guilty plea
key_facts: Carl Mason pleaded guilty to manslaughter as an alternative to murder after a street attack in York killed Michael Brolly.
Crown case included CCTV and eyewitness evidence that Mason joined kicks to the prone victim.
Mason later sought twice to vacate the plea alleging pressure from co-defendants and counsel.
At sentencing stage prosecution could not call key witness Croft due to subsequent misconduct allegations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against conviction after refusal to vacate guilty plea and against sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal against conviction dismissed; the judge's discretion on both vacation applications was not vitiated by error of principle.
enrichment.ratio: A change of plea from guilty to not guilty requires an objective basis and sparing exercise of discretion; counsel may advise firmly provided the defendant's choice remains free, and subsequent weakening of prosecution evidence after an unequivocal plea does not automatically permit vacation where the plea remained a voluntary acceptance of participation in unlawful violence.
legal_issues: Whether the guilty plea was freely and genuinely made
Whether improper pressure from co-defendants or counsel vitiated the plea
Whether later doubts about witness Croft justified changing the plea
Application of Recorder of Manchester principles at sentencing stage

Turner [1970] 2 QBD 321

notes: QB trust and knowing receipt trial judgment in dispute over Iraqi refugee funds invested in property; BCCI v Akindele applied.

enrichment.short_title: Ali v Al-Basri: breach of trust and knowing receipt of refugee funds
key_facts: Iraqi-born claimant Souad Ali entrusted large sums to Akeel Al-Basri after arriving in the UK in 1993.
Al-Basri invested deposits in several properties, including Sullivan Court bought largely in his wife's name.
The claimant said funds were held on trust; the first defendant claimed repayment or a personal loan.
The second defendant said she believed the money was an informal loan from a family friend.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Queen's Bench Division on claims for breach of trust, knowing receipt and related proprietary relief.
enrichment.outcome: Claim upheld against the second defendant in respect of Sullivan Court and Copley Close; she holds legal title on trust for the claimant, with further accounting needed for other properties.
enrichment.ratio: A recipient's knowledge must make it unconscionable to retain benefit; where funds were manifestly entrusted rather than lent and invested in property, a spouse with actual knowledge and agency attribution holds acquired property on constructive trust despite denials of involvement.
legal_issues: Whether money was held on trust or lent to the first defendant
Whether the second defendant had requisite knowledge for knowing receipt
Attribution of the first defendant's knowledge as her agent
Whether sanctions evasion barred equitable relief

Pickering v McConville [2003] EWCA Civ 554

notes: Admin judgment on Dublin Convention screening, Article 15 humanitarian clause and clearly unfounded human rights certification for Somali asylum seeker.

enrichment.short_title: R (G) v SSHD: Dublin transfer, Regulation 343/2003 and Article 8 certificate
key_facts: Somali claimant sought asylum in the UK after earlier claiming asylum in Italy detected via Eurodac.
Secretary of State certified Italy as responsible state and decided to remove her to Italy.
She later claimed Article 8 family life with a cousin in the UK and disputed her age.
Certificate that the human rights claim was clearly unfounded removed in-country appeal rights.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of a clearly unfounded certificate under section 93 of the 2002 Act preventing an in-country appeal against removal to Italy.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Dublin screening is conducted once on facts at first application and cannot be rerun in the UK; Article 6 and 7 criteria did not make the UK responsible, Article 15 confers only a discretionary humanitarian power exercisable at Italy's request, and the Secretary of State could rationally reject the Article 8 claim as clearly unfounded on the evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the UK remained responsible under Dublin II Regulation Articles 6 and 7
Whether screening could be repeated after Italy accepted responsibility
Construction of Article 15 humanitarian clause and guardian for unaccompanied minors
Lawfulness of clearly unfounded certification under Article 8
linked_authorities: R (Ekinci) v SSHD [2003] EWCA Civ 765
R (Mahmood) v SSHD [2001] 1 WLR 840

notes: Crim CA dismissal of misconduct in public office appeal by Lincolnshire council leader over A1073 route influence; costs order reduced.

enrichment.short_title: R v Speechley: misconduct in public office over road re-alignment
key_facts: County council leader Jim Speechley owned a four-acre field near Crowland affected by an A1073 bypass re-alignment.
He influenced the proposed route without declaring his interest and marked his land on plans shown to officers.
A jury convicted him of misconduct in public office with dishonesty as the driving motive.
He was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment and ordered to pay £25,000 prosecution costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against conviction and sentence for common law misconduct in public office.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed; sentence of 18 months upheld but prosecution costs contribution reduced from £25,000 to £10,000.
enrichment.ratio: Misconduct in public office requires serious improper conduct impugning public interest; where dishonesty was the driving force in influencing a public project for personal advantage, mixed motives do not assist unless honest motives were sole drivers, and juries may not be invited to acquit mid-trial without judicial invitation.
legal_issues: Correct mental element and direction on mixed motives
Whether no case to answer should have been upheld
Whether defence could remind jury of mid-trial acquittal right
Appropriateness of 18-month sentence and prosecution costs order

R v Dytham [1979] 1 QB 722
R v Galbraith (1981) 73 Cr App R 124

notes: Commercial Court ruling on joinder of assignee to avoid security for costs; Eurocross/Norglen bind the court.

enrichment.short_title: Noga v ANZ: equitable assignment and security for costs
key_facts: Swiss company Noga pursued tracing claims over Nigerian bill-of-exchange proceeds against banks and intermediaries.
Impecunious Noga assigned equitable interests in the claims to principal shareholder Nessim Gaon to seek joinder.
Defendants applied for security for costs against both Noga and Gaon after long-standing litigation delays.
ANZ remained subject to an unfulfilled £112,500 security order from a 1999 consent order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications in the Commercial Court to join Mr Gaon as claimant and for security for costs against Noga and/or Gaon.
enrichment.outcome: Gaon joined as co-claimant subject only to security for costs thrown away by joinder; no further security ordered against Noga beyond existing ANZ order; applications against Gaon under CPR 25.13(2)(f) and (g) refused.
enrichment.ratio: Joinder of an equitable assignee is desirable to bind assignor and assignee, but conditions cannot require an individual assignee to provide security that would restore company-level protection; Eurocross and Norglen preclude using joinder to impose security on an impecunious individual where the company claim would otherwise be stifled, though Noga failed to prove stifling on candid disclosure.
legal_issues: Validity and effect of equitable assignment of tracing claims
Whether joinder should be conditional on security for costs
Jurisdiction under CPR 25.13(2)(c), (f) and (g)
Whether assignment was an abuse of process to evade security

Norglen Ltd v Reeds Rains Prudential Ltd [1999] 2 AC 1

notes: Planning JR holding enforcement appeal invalid where notice identified withdrawn notice A1 rather than reissued notice A2.

enrichment.short_title: McKay v FSS: invalid planning enforcement appeal after withdrawn notice

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995

key_facts: Claimant created vehicular access and parking at The Beacon, Penn, believing works were permitted development.
Wycombe District Council served enforcement notices A and B on 22 December 2003, then withdrew notice A1 and reissued notice A2 on 23 December correcting a plan defect.
The agent's appeal form dated notice A as 22 December 2003 and appended withdrawn notice A1.
Appeal papers arrived on 3 February 2004; the Inspectorate later held the appeal invalid after the council pointed out the error.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of an Inspectorate decision that the enforcement appeal was invalid.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 174 requires written notice identifying the enforcement notice appealed against; where the appeal expressly referred to the withdrawn notice and appended it, the Inspectorate could not treat the appeal as relating to the reissued notice without jurisdiction to substitute an out-of-time appeal.
legal_issues: Whether section 174 requires identification of the specific enforcement notice
Whether an obvious agent's mistake permits objective reinterpretation of the appeal
Whether the Inspectorate could substitute notice A2 for notice A1
Effect of withdrawal and reissue under section 173A
linked_authorities: Howard v Secretary of State for the Environment [1975] 1 QB 235
Cala Homes (South) Ltd v Chichester District Council [1999] 79 P&CR 430
